loText: Identify and discuss various factors that affect the choice of investment securities by a bank.
question: A senior risk analyst at a US bank is drafting a section on inflation risk for the board’s annual review of the investment policy. Which of the following statements should the analyst include as most accurate?

options.A: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities protect holders against all effects of inflation, including a drift into higher tax brackets.
options.B: Long-term fixed-rate bonds give the investments officer the most flexibility to respond to any flare-up in inflationary pressures.
options.C: When expected inflation falls, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities tend to become more valuable to investors than before.
options.D: The yield spread between conventional Treasury notes and inflation-protected Treasuries of the same maturity provides an index of expected inflation.

solution:
Inflation risk statements for the board’s investment policy review.

**Concept and theory**

Inflation risk is the possibility that rising prices for goods and services erode the purchasing power of the interest income and repaid principal from a security or loan. GARP adds that inflation can also erode the value of the stockholders’ investment in the financial firm, its net worth.

Some protection comes from short-term securities and those with variable interest rates, which give the investments officer greater flexibility to respond to any flare-up in inflationary pressures. A more direct hedge is the US Treasury’s Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), issued since 1997 in 5-, 10- and 30-year maturities, whose principal is adjusted to match changes in the consumer price index.

options.A: It reduces fluctuations in investment income and requires little expertise, although it does not maximize investment income.

question: The CRO of a large Brazilian bank with a dedicated economics department reviews the bank’s BRL 12 billion securities portfolio. The bank manages maturities under a rate expectations approach, and the latest house forecast is that market interest rates will rise significantly over the next year. Which of the following best describes how the approach should be applied and what it entails?

options.A: Shift toward the long end of the maturity spectrum, because rising rates are expected to generate capital gains on longer-term securities.
options.B: Shift toward the short end of the maturity spectrum, accepting greater transactions costs from the frequent trading and switching the approach requires.

Large Brazilian bank using a rate expectations approach faces a forecast of rising rates.

GARP calls the rate expectations (or total performance) approach “the most aggressive of all maturity strategies”, often used by the largest financial firms. Instead of fixing a maturity structure, the institution continually shifts the maturities of its securities in line with current forecasts of interest rates and the economy.

The logic rests on the inverse relation between rates and bond prices, with the longest maturities moving most. If rates are expected to rise, longer-term securities will suffer the largest capital losses, so the portfolio is shifted toward the short end of the maturity spectrum. UK bank board paper: which justification for a loss-making securities sale is least appropriate?

Trading securities before maturity is the operational side of the rate expectations approach. GARP notes that banks often trade some of their unpledged holdings whenever there is the prospect of significant gains in expected returns or the opportunity to reduce asset risk without significant loss in expected yield, and they are particularly aggressive when loan revenues are down. But losses on security trades reduce before-tax income, so portfolio managers do not like to take losses unless they can show the board that the loss will be more than made up by higher expected returns on the new assets bought with the proceeds.

question:
A portfolio manager at a Singapore bank observes the following government yield curve. The bank’s effective corporate tax rate is 17%.

| Maturity | Yield (%) |
|---|---|
| 3 months | 3.60 |
| 1 year | 3.40 |
| 2 years | 3.15 |
| 5 years | 2.90 |
| 10 years | 2.75 |

Using the yield curve as an interest rate forecasting tool, which of the following conclusions and actions is most appropriate for the SGD investment portfolio?

options.A: The curve reflects an expectation that future short-term rates will be higher, so the manager should shorten portfolio maturity.
options.B: The curve reflects an expectation of declining short-term rates, so the manager should shorten portfolio maturity to avoid capital losses.

GARP (Section 4.9) introduces the yield curve as a picture of how market interest rates differ across securities of varying term to maturity, with all yields measured at the same time and all other rate-determining forces held fixed. It may slope upward, slope downward, or be horizontal.

The first use GARP describes is forecasting: the yield curve “contains an implicit forecast of future interest rate changes.”

question: A treasury analyst at a US bank is evaluating a carry trade. The bank would borrow USD 80 million for 30 days at 4.10% (annualized), pledging Treasury bills as collateral, and roll the borrowing at the same rate for one year. The proceeds would buy 5-year government notes yielding 5.35%. Custody and dealer fees on the position are 0.15% per year. The 10-year government yield is 5.60%. options.A: USD 0.07 million
options.B: USD 1.00 million

options.D: USD 1.08 million

US bank: annual carry return from borrowing short at 4.10% to hold 5-year notes at 5.35%, net of 0.15% fees.

The carry trade is GARP’s fourth yield-curve tool. The officer borrows at the short end of the curve (for example, short-term money raised using the safest and most liquid securities in the portfolio as collateral) and invests the borrowed funds in income-generating assets farther out the curve. GARP’s example: borrow for 30 days at 4% and buy five-year government bonds yielding 6%. The difference between the two rates is called **carry income**, and it tends to be greatest when the yield curve has a steep upward slope.

question:
The CCO of a Canadian trust company is reviewing training slides on maturity management tools prepared for newly hired investment analysts. The slides make the following statements:

I. The yield curve counts only clock time to maturity, not the timing and amount of the cash flows a security will generate.

II. The shape of the yield curve can change at any time, which can undermine strategies built on its current shape.

III. Duration is a present-value-weighted measure of maturity that indicates the average time needed for all of a security’s cash flows to reach the investor.

IV. Unlike duration, the yield curve tells the investments officer how much cash a security will generate in each period it is held.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, II, III and IV
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I, II and III only

solution:
Training slides: limitations of the yield curve and the definition of duration.

**Concept and theory**

GARP closes its yield-curve discussion with the tool’s limitations, and these are what motivate duration.

- There is uncertainty over exactly how and why the curve looks the way it does at any moment.
- The curve’s shape may change at any time (Schweser: slope and steepness can change and adversely affect portfolio values).
- The yield curve “counts only clock time”, not the timing of cash flows expected from a security.

question:
Loan demand at a Canadian bank is currently weak, so its investments officer plans to buy CAD 60 million of government securities now. She expects to sell them in exactly three years to fund new loans, and she wants to minimize interest rate risk over that holding period. The candidates are:

| Security | Description | Yield (%) | Duration (years) |
|---|---|---|---|
| W | 1-year bill | 4.70 | 1.00 |
| X | 3-year note, 6% annual coupon | 5.00 | 2.84 |
| Y | 3-year zero-coupon note | 5.05 | 3.00 |
| Z | 7-year note, 6.5% annual coupon | 5.60 | 5.87 |

Which choice best immunizes the planned investment?

options.A: Security Y, because its duration equals the planned three-year holding period.
options.B: Security X, because its maturity equals the planned three-year holding period.
options.C: Security Z, because its higher yield will offset any price loss over the holding period.
options.D: Security W, because the shortest duration minimizes price risk and so immunizes the return.

solution:
Canadian bank with a three-year holding period chooses which security immunizes the investment.

**Concept and theory**

Duration gives the investments officer a tool to reduce exposure to interest rate risk. GARP’s formula for minimizing interest rate risk (Equation 4.9) is simply

Duration of a security or portfolio = Length of the investor’s planned holding period.

GARP’s illustration is close to this question: a bank buys Treasury notes because loan demand is weak, but the officer may need to sell them in a year to make loans, so the officer chooses notes with a duration of one year. This is **portfolio immunization**: protecting the return on securities purchased from loss, no matter which way interest rates go.

question:
A member of the risk committee of a Singapore bank is reviewing a proposal to immunize a SGD 500 million bond portfolio by setting its duration equal to the bank’s planned holding period. The committee paper makes the following statements:

I. If rates rise after purchase, the portfolio’s market value falls, but its cash flows can be reinvested at higher rates, so the two effects approximately offset.

II. Immunization works because price risk and reinvestment risk respond in opposite directions to a change in interest rates.

III. Immunization protects the return only when rates fall; when rates rise, the capital loss dominates the reinvestment gain.

IV. Matching duration to the holding period freezes the total return exactly, whatever the size of the rate change.

options.D: II and III only

| Rates rise | Market value falls (capital loss) | Cash flows reinvested at higher rates |

A member of the risk committee at a Canadian credit union is drafting the definition of “liquidity” for the committee charter. The draft must also state whether a well-capitalized institution can fail for liquidity reasons alone.

Which of the following drafts is most accurate?

options.A: A firm is liquid if it can obtain immediately spendable funds at whatever price the market sets, at precisely the time they are needed; a technically solvent firm can still be closed for lack of liquidity.
options.B: A firm is liquid if it has ready access to immediately spendable funds at reasonable cost, at precisely the time they are needed; a technically solvent firm can still be closed for lack of liquidity.
options.C: A firm is liquid if it has ready access to immediately spendable funds at reasonable cost, which a large enough stock of liquid assets always guarantees; a technically solvent firm can still be closed for lack of liquidity.

Risk committee member drafting the definition of liquidity and stating whether a solvent firm can fail for liquidity reasons.

| Immediately spendable funds | Assets or credit that cannot be turned into cash quickly enough |
| Reasonable cost | Funds that are technically obtainable only at a punitive rate or with a large loss on asset sales |

question:

I. Drawings by corporate customers on their existing credit lines are a demand for liquidity, just as new loan requests the bank wishes to grant are.

II. Repaying an advance the bank previously received from the central bank is a demand for liquidity.

The institution’s demand for liquidity is therefore driven by its customers’ own cash needs, and stress in the customer base turns into stress for the lender.
